analysis.investment_thesis: Eureka Forbes owns the iconic Aquaguard brand in a structurally growing water purification market, with improving profitability (Net Profit: ₹26 Cr → ₹164 Cr in 3 years) and virtually zero debt. However, at 47x P/E with ROE of merely 3.7% and single-digit revenue growth (~8% CAGR FY23-25), the valuation demands perfection that current fundamentals don't yet justify.
key_strengths: Iconic Aquaguard brand with deep distribution and ~10 million AMC customers providing recurring revenue — classic moat in underpenetrated water purification market
Pristine balance sheet: Debt/Equity of 0.02, Total Debt just ₹26 Cr vs. equity of ₹4,520 Cr; FCF growing steadily to ₹190 Cr in FY25
Profitability inflecting sharply — Operating Income tripled from ₹88 Cr (FY22) to ₹266 Cr (FY25); gross margin of 59% shows brand pricing power
key_risks: PE ownership by Advent International (via Lunolux, 62.56%) creates persistent stake-sale overhang — not an owner-operator promoter story I like
Revenue growth of ~8% CAGR (FY23-FY25) is well below my 15-20% threshold for a 47x P/E stock; market is pricing in acceleration that isn't yet visible
ROE of 3.71% and ROCE of 5.07% are embarrassingly low — equity base inflated by acquisition goodwill, but capital productivity remains poor regardless of the explanation
red_flags: PE firm as promoter — eventual exit/block deal risk can suppress stock price for years
P/E of 47.3x with sub-10% revenue growth and sub-5% ROCE is a dangerous combination — paying a luxury valuation for a mid-tier compounder
Operating margin of only 8% despite 59% gross margin signals extremely high distribution/SG&A costs from the direct sales model — structural ceiling on profitability
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Eureka Forbes is a good business, not a great one. Aquaguard is a household name in India, and water purification is a genuine long-term secular story aligned with India's consumption and health awareness themes. The profitability turnaround since re-listing in FY22 is real — net profit has grown 6x in three years and FCF conversion is excellent (₹190 Cr FCF vs. ₹164 Cr net profit). The balance sheet is squeaky clean with near-zero debt. These are things I appreciate.

But the price I am being asked to pay is simply not justified. At 47x P/E, the market is pricing this as a high-growth compounder, yet revenue grew only ~11% in FY25 and ~5% in FY24. ROE of 3.7% would be unacceptable in any business, even accounting for goodwill inflation post-Advent acquisition. The real killer for me is the promoter structure — Advent International is a financial sponsor, not an owner-operator. They will exit eventually, and when they do, the stock will face severe selling pressure. I want promoters who have built a business over decades and are still hungry to grow it, not a PE firm managing a portfolio company toward an IPO exit. Wait for ROE to cross 12%, revenue growth to consistently hit 15%+, and a more sensible P/E of 20-25x before revisiting.
